Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 97, verse 1:

(p-182) Surat al-Qadr (The Surah of Power/Decree)

It is a Meccan surah, though this is disputed, and its verses number five.

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Power.﴾ This is an exaltation of the status of the Noble Qur'an and a glorification of its rank, by means of the pronoun referring back to it, which signals the utmost prominence of its subject, dispensing with the need to name it explicitly, as though it were present in every mind; and by ascribing its sending down to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), which indicates the utmost care given to it; and by magnifying the time of its sending down through the words of the Exalted:

﴿And what will make you comprehend what the Night of Decree is?﴾ This indicates that the sublimity of its rank lies beyond the scope of created understanding. No one knows it or can make it known except the Knower of the unseen, as is indicated by the words of Allah, exalted is He:

﴿Laylat al-Qadr is better than a thousand months﴾. This is a general statement of its status, following his (peace be upon him) arousing interest in knowing it, since that indicates a promise to make it known. The explanation of how the two sentences are parsed (i'rab, the grammatical analysis of the sentence) has already been given. Repeating "Laylat al-Qadr" in both places (instead of using a pronoun) emphasizes its greatness, which is obvious.

As for the meaning of "We sent it down in it": either the whole (Qur'an) was sent down to the lowest heaven, as is narrated, that it was sent down all at once on Laylat al-Qadr from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) to the lowest heaven, and Jibril (peace be upon him) dictated it to the scribes (al-safara), and then he would send it down upon the Prophet (ﷺ) in installments over twenty-three years; or the beginning of its being sent down was in it, as is reported from al-Sha'bi. It has also been said that the meaning is: We sent it down concerning the matter of Laylat al-Qadr and its virtue, as in the words of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "I feared that a Qur'an would be revealed concerning me," and the words of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her): "I consider myself too insignificant for a Qur'an to be revealed concerning me." In that case, the most fitting interpretation is that the pronoun refers to the surah, which is a part of the Qur'an, not to the whole.

They differed about its time. Most of them hold that it is in the month of Ramadan, in the last ten nights, in the odd ones, and most of the opinions say it is the seventh of them. Perhaps the wisdom in concealing it is to encourage the one who seeks it to obtain great reward by worshipping through many nights, hoping to coincide with it.

Its being named "al-Qadr" is either because the affairs are measured and decreed in it, in accordance with the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿In it every wise matter is decreed﴾, or because of its worth and nobility above the other nights.

The mention of "a thousand" is singled out either for the sake of expressing abundance, or because of what is reported: the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned a man from the Children of Israel who wore weapons in the way of Allah for a thousand months, so the believers were amazed by him and their own deeds seemed small to them, so they were given a night that is better than the duration of that warrior. It has also been said that a man in former times was called "worshipper" ('abid) only once he had worshipped Allah the Exalted for a thousand months, so they were given a night which, if they spent it in worship, would make them more deserving of being called worshippers than those worshippers. It has also been said that the Prophet (ﷺ) was shown the lifespans of all the nations, and he considered the lifespan of his own community too short, and feared that they would not attain as much deeds as others attained through long life, so Allah gave him Laylat al-Qadr and made it better than a thousand months for all the other nations. It has also been said: the kingdom of Sulayman was five hundred months, and the kingdom of Dhu al-Qarnayn was five hundred months, so Allah the Exalted made the deed on this night for whoever attains it better than their kingdom combined.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 97, verse 4:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾. This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining the basis of its (the night's) excellence over that lengthy period. What has been said concerning the Spirit in detail has already passed in Surat al-Naba'. It has also been said: they are a kind of angel whom the (other) angels do not see except on that night. That is, the angels and the Spirit descend in that night from every heaven to the earth, or to the lowest heaven.

﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾ relates to "descend" (tanazzalu), or to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, meaning: accompanied by the permission of their Lord, that is, by His command. ﴿For every matter﴾ means: on account of every matter that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has decreed for that year until the next, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In it every wise matter is decided﴾. It has been read as "min kulli imri'" (for every person), meaning: on account of every human being. It has been said: they do not meet in it any believing man or believing woman without greeting them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 97, verse 5:**

﴿Peace it is﴾ — that is, it is nothing but peace; that is, Allah the Exalted decrees in it only peace and goodness, whereas in other nights He decrees both peace and affliction. Or it means: it is nothing but peace, because of the abundance of those who greet the believers with peace therein. ﴿Until the rising of the dawn﴾ — that is, until the time of its rising. It is also read with a kasra (*mat'la'*, *matla'*), being a verbal noun like *al-marji'* (the return), or a noun of time by irregular derivation like *al-mashriq* (the place of sunrise). And "until" (*hatta*) is connected to "descend" (*tanazzalu*), as an end point for the ruling of the descent; that is, for their remaining in the place of their descent, or for the descent itself, such that their descent does not cease, company after company, until the rising of the dawn. It has also been said that it is connected to "peace" (*salam*), on the basis that separating the verbal noun from its complement by the subject is permissible when the separator is a prepositional phrase.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Qadr will be given a reward like that of one who fasted Ramadan and spent the Night of Decree in worship."
